protections: setIn must not let a caller-supplied path step out of the target object's own data into a shared built-in object (Object.prototype via __proto__ or constructor.prototype, or other inherited built-ins); the only key handling today is the '-' array-append rewrite at index.js:21-24 and the unconditional write at index.js:32

traps.note: A path element '__proto__' is used unchecked. Line 26 reads object['__proto__'], which resolves to the shared prototype, and line 32 writes into it. This is the CVE-2020-28273 route that a report would describe directly.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: after adding a '__proto__' check, a ['constructor','prototype',...] path contains no forbidden literal
traps.note: Nested form: two inherited hops reach the same shared prototype. This is the likely shape of the later advisory, B (incomplete fix). At the pinned commit no guard exists, so a solver given both reports would fix both at once.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: a strict-equality check against the string '__proto__' looks complete because keys are 'strings'
traps.note: Non-string key shapes, such as an array element ['__proto__'] or an object with a toString method, coerce to the dangerous property name at the bracket access on lines 26/32. A plausible check `key === '__proto__'` (the same idiom as line 21) misses them.

traps.reason_to_dismiss: the path never names __proto__/constructor.prototype, so Object.prototype itself is untouched; writes land on a built-in function such as Object.prototype.toString or on the Object constructor
traps.note: Wrong object: traversal at line 26 descends into any inherited value, such as object.toString, object.hasOwnProperty or object.constructor, which are shared built-ins. It then writes a property onto that shared object at line 32 before reassigning it as an own property at line 28. A denylist of __proto__/constructor/prototype does not close the toString/hasOwnProperty variants; an own-property check does.

conflicts.what: A blanket ban on the key 'constructor' (the natural fix for T2/T4) also refuses a harmless own data key 'constructor' as the final path element. Nothing in test/ covers that key, so whether it must keep working is unverified.

fairness_risks: Creating missing intermediate objects must keep working (test/index.js:92-113, a deep unresolved path, built via index.js:17). A fix that refuses to descend into non-own properties must still create {} for absent keys rather than throw.

Numeric array indices and the '-' append key must keep working (test/index.js:47-69, index.js:21-24). A fix that only accepts string keys, or rejects non-string keys outright, would break numeric paths. Any T3 hardening must coerce keys before comparing them rather than refusing numbers.
Keys named 'constructor' or 'prototype' as legitimate own data fields would be refused by a denylist fix; the published fixes likely do this too (unverified).

design.why: Not usable as a stacked task. The whole package is one 34-line file with one sink (index.js:26/32). A single fix in recursivelySetIn, such as String(key) checked against a denylist plus an own-property check before descending, closes every trap. At most 2 independent groups exist (name denylist vs inherited-traversal), short of 3-5. At the pinned commit (2.0.0, before fix A) both advisories are open together, so the A->B incomplete-fix history adds no separate judgement. If it must be used, the best that can be built is T1+T2 as the advisory surface, T4 as the deepseek-type trap (no forbidden name appears, so it is dismissable as not real prototype pollution) and T3 as the mimo-type trap (how-type key coercion). Even so, they share one fix site and one function.

unverified: Content of fix A (e431effa0019, CVE-2020-28273) and fix B (6bad255961d3): the pinned commit a883c87 (version 2.0.0, package.json:3) predates both. From public knowledge only, A added a '__proto__' path check and B extended or replaced it because the check could be bypassed (e.g. a constructor/prototype path or an overridable Array.prototype.includes). Not verified against code here, so a_fix_leaves_b_open and b_in_code_a_wrote are left null.

Whether B lives in code A wrote (regression of A's guard) vs elsewhere: the advisory 'link' says incomplete fix, which suggests B bypasses A's guard in the same function index.js:12-29, but this is not visible at the pinned commit.
Whether upstream's final fix also blocks the T4 inherited-built-in route (toString/hasOwnProperty) or only a name denylist.
No dependency-bump fix: package.json:34 has no runtime dependencies, so any fix must be in-repo.
